How a Tonne of SO₂ Becomes Sunlight Reflected

an interactive companion to Linz, Akherati, et al., "Process Uncertainties for SO₂-to-Aerosol Transformation in Stratospheric Aerosol Injection" · built from the paper's own model runs

The abstract, annotated

the paper's own words · every highlighted claim opens its chapter

Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) is a proposed tool for reducing climate risks by reflecting sunlight to cool the Earth's surface, but significant new research is needed to support informed societal decisions about its use. The most commonly assumed SAI approach uses aircraft to loft SO₂ to the stratosphere, where the SO₂ gas would oxidize and form sulfate aerosols. However, modern climate models, from which SAI impact assessments are made, do not capture the details of the small-scale processes involved in aerosol formation. Observations after large volcanic eruptions can help constrain models for SAI studies, but injection from stratospheric aircraft has significant differences from an eruption. We discuss how SO₂ released behind an airplane mixes, oxidizes, and forms aerosols, identify uncertainties of each process, and propagate them through a plume aerosol microphysical model for up to 10 days, concluding that there is considerable uncertainty in the aerosol size distribution that would result from aircraft-released SO₂. The largest uncertainties arise from mixing and new particle formation, but even the comparatively modest uncertainty in coagulation has a larger effect on the resulting size distribution than a three-order-of-magnitude-larger uncertainty in nucleation. We discuss why key uncertainties cannot be addressed solely via indoor experiments or modeling, and thus why substantively reducing uncertainty related to aerosol microphysics would require small-scale field experimentation to better understand the relevant processes and their interactions.

Climate models are how we judge stratospheric aerosol injection. But a released plume starts ten meters wide, and a climate model cannot see anything smaller than its grid cell, roughly a hundred kilometers across. Slide from the model's world down to the airplane's.

Why volcanoes are not enough

Mount Pinatubo put 15 to 20 million tonnes of SO₂ into the stratosphere in a single day and cooled the planet by roughly 0.3 to 0.5 °C the following year. That natural experiment anchors much of what we know.

An aircraft releases fifty tonnes or less into a ribbon ten meters wide. Every step of the chemistry and microphysics depends on concentration, so a narrow, slowly diluting ribbon evolves differently from a volcanic cloud a thousand times more massive. The analog helps; it does not close the case.

The life of the sulfur, left to right

How fast the plume mixes into clean air is the biggest unknown of all, and it feeds every other process. The paper derives a simple law for it, built from wind shear tilting the plume and turbulence mixing across the tilt. Try it.

Dilution, days one through ten

V(t)/V₀ = how many times over the plume has been diluted · model regimes shown for reference

The pilot's lever

Wind speed changes with height, so the plume gets tilted into a long, thin sheet. Turbulence then mixes across that sheet. Fly the release along the shear and the plume stays concentrated for days; fly across it and dilution is dramatically faster. The choice belongs to whoever plans the flight. It is a design lever, not just an uncertainty.

The catch: the mixing strength Kz is known only to within a factor of about a thousand. At one week, the strong and weak ends of that range differ by three orders of magnitude in dilution.

Inside the plume, chemistry keeps daylight hours. Sunlight makes OH, OH turns SO₂ into sulfuric acid, and the acid becomes particles. Pick a case; every curve is a real model run.

Here is the counterintuitive part. Nucleation rates are uncertain by a factor of ten thousand; coagulation by maybe a factor of four. Flip the switches and watch which one actually moves the answer.

Size distribution

· dSA/dlogDp, dry

×10,000 → ×2
the full nucleation uncertainty changes climate-relevant particle numbers by only about a factor of two: the system buffers it
×4 → largest shift
coagulation's modest range moves the size distribution more than any other knob, and it keeps acting long after the chemistry is done
α: barely visible
halving the condensation coefficient feeds back on the acid vapor and nearly cancels itself out

The buffering works like this: make nucleation faster and you get more, smaller particles competing for the same acid vapor. They grow slower and get swallowed by bigger particles faster. The errors largely cancel. Coagulation has no such counterweight; it runs day and night, for the entire life of the aerosol. Well understood is not the same as unimportant.

Some of these gaps yield to computers and laboratory chambers. Some do not. The paper's conclusion is that the integrated question, what a real release actually becomes, can only be answered by releasing a small amount and measuring it.

The scoreboard

What a small-release experiment looks like

An aircraft in the stratosphere releases SO₂ at deployment-like rates, one to five tonnes per minute, leaving a plume roughly 25 kilometers long from a payload of ten tonnes or less. The plume is tracked by forecast models and remote sensing, then sampled repeatedly until the SO₂ has oxidized or the plume has blended into the background.

Chambers cannot reach stratospheric humidity. Models of plume dilution have never been validated at these scales. Balloons can probe mixing but not the chemistry. Each closes part of the gap; only a release closes the loop. There is precedent: it was aircraft measurements inside the Antarctic ozone hole, not models alone, that settled that science and convinced the world to act.
